title: Trading, market structure, settlement, and the regulatory back end

reading.h: The 1934 Act back end and issuer reporting
reading.body:
The Securities Exchange Act of 1934 governs everything after a security is issued. It requires public companies to keep the market informed with periodic reports: the **10-K** (annual, audited), the **10-Q** (quarterly, unaudited), and the **8-K** (a material event, filed within **4 business days**). These are disclosure documents — the SEC reviews for completeness, never approves the company.

The Act also created the SEC, requires registration of exchanges and broker-dealers, sets anti-fraud Rule 10b-5, the net-capital and customer-protection rules (15c3-1 and 15c3-3), and delegated margin authority to the Fed. Think of it as the rulebook for the ongoing life of a security and the people who trade it.

reading.h: Section 16 vs. 13D/13G vs. insider trading — three separate things
reading.body:
These three sound alike and are constantly confused; keep them as three separate dashboards. **Section 16 = insiders' paperwork and profit clawback.** Insiders are officers, directors, and **>10%** owners. They file Form 3 (within 10 days of becoming an insider), Form 4 (within **2 business days** of a change), and Form 5. The **short-swing profit rule 16(b)** lets the issuer recover any profit from a purchase and sale within **6 months**, regardless of intent.

**Sections 13(d)/(g) = big buyers announcing themselves.** Acquiring more than **5%** of a class with intent to influence control triggers a **Schedule 13D**; a passive investor files the shorter **Schedule 13G**. **Insider trading = using secrets.** Trading on material nonpublic information in breach of a duty is illegal; intent matters, and civil penalties reach **treble (3×)** the profit gained or loss avoided, on top of criminal exposure. In one line: 16 is paperwork and a no-fault clawback; 13D is a disclosure of a big stake; insider trading is fraud.

Every sell order must be marked **long, short, or short-exempt** (Rule 200), and a seller is "long" only if it owns and can deliver the shares. Before any short sale, the broker-dealer must **locate** the shares — borrow, arrange to borrow, or reasonably believe they can be borrowed for settlement (Rule 203).

**Rule 201 (the short-sale circuit breaker):** when an NMS stock drops **10%** from the prior close, for the rest of that day and the next day short sales may execute only at a price **above the national best bid**. A stock lands on the **threshold list** when fails reach both **10,000 shares and 0.5% of shares outstanding** for 5 straight settlement days. Short sales must be done in a margin account. The old "uptick tick test" was abolished in 2007 — don't pick it.

reading.h: Market structure: NYSE, Nasdaq, OTC, and Reg NMS
reading.body:
The **NYSE** is an **auction** market: buyers compete with buyers, and one **Designated Market Maker (DMM)** per stock runs the auctions and maintains a fair and orderly market (replacing the old "specialist"). **Nasdaq** is a **dealer** market of competing **market makers** posting firm two-sided quotes; the display levels are **Level 1** (best bid/ask), **Level 2** (every market maker's quotes), and **Level 3** (a market maker's own entry terminal).

"OTC" now means non-exchange-listed; OTC Markets tiers are OTCQX, OTCQB, and Pink (the OTCBB ceased operation in 2021 — treat it as history). **Alternative trading systems (ATSs)** — ECNs and dark pools — register as broker-dealers under Reg ATS. **Regulation NMS** ties the markets together: **Rule 611 (order protection / trade-through)** bars executing at a worse price than a protected quote elsewhere, and the **NBBO** is the best bid and offer across all venues.

reading.h: Order types and reading the tape
reading.body:
A **market order** guarantees execution, not price. A **limit order** guarantees price (or better), not execution. A **stop order** is dormant until a print **at or through** the stop price **elects** it, after which it becomes a **market order** and fills at the next price. A **stop-limit** elects the same way but becomes a **limit order** — so in a fast market it may never fill.

Placement mnemonic: orders **below** the market are **B**uy **Li**mit and **S**ell **S**top ("BLiSS"); orders **above** are **S**ell **L**imit and **B**uy **S**top ("SLoBS"). Because the ex-dividend price drops, **Rule 5330** reduces only the below-market (BLiSS) open orders by the dividend on the ex-date, rounding down to the next lower valid tick — unless marked **DNR**. Above-market orders are not adjusted; stock splits adjust everything; reverse splits cancel open orders.

A firm acts as **agent/broker** (matches the customer with another party, charges a disclosed **commission**) or as **principal/dealer** (trades from inventory, earns a **markup/markdown** in the price) — never both on one trade. A **riskless principal** buys only after receiving the customer's order and resells immediately, so its markup is measured off its **contemporaneous cost**, not old inventory, and (for equities) must be disclosed.

**FINRA Rule 2121 — the 5% policy** — is a **guideline**, not a hard cap: markups must be fair and reasonable given security type, liquidity, price, and trade size. The base is the **prevailing market (inside) price**, never the dealer's cost; **disclosure does not cure** an excessive markup; **municipals and new issues are excluded**. **Confirmations (Rule 10b-10)** are due at or before completion of the transaction (settlement) and must show the firm's capacity, the commission if agent, whether the firm is a market maker, and payment-for-order-flow disclosure.

Regular-way settlement is **T+1** for essentially everything — stocks, corporate and municipal bonds, Treasuries, options, and funds (moved from T+2 on May 28, 2024). **Cash settlement** is same-day. **Reg T payment** is due **T+3** (settlement + 2); if a customer doesn't pay, the firm liquidates and freezes the account for **90 days**. Behind the scenes, **DTCC** subsidiaries do the plumbing: **NSCC** clears and nets trades, **DTC** is the central depository, and the **OCC** issues and guarantees listed options.

Trade-reporting timing is heavily tested: **TRACE** (corporate/agency bonds) and **RTRS** (munis) both require reporting within **15 minutes** (the proposed 1-minute standard was rescinded in 2025). The **TRF** (listed stocks traded off-exchange) and **ORF** (non-listed OTC equities) require reporting within **10 seconds**. Volatility brakes are three separate systems: market-wide **circuit breakers** on the S&P 500 (−7%/−13% → 15-minute halt if before 3:25 pm ET; −20% → closed for the day), single-stock **LULD** price bands, and Reg SHO Rule 201.

flashcards.front: Regular-way settlement and Reg T payment
flashcards.back: Regular way = T+1 (all products since 5/28/2024); cash = same day; Reg T payment = T+3; unpaid → 90-day freeze.
TRACE (corp/agency bonds) and RTRS (munis) = 15 minutes; TRF (listed off-exchange) and ORF (OTC equities) = 10 seconds; CAT next trading day.
−7% (L1) / −13% (L2) → 15-minute halt only if before 3:25 pm ET; −20% (L3) → market closed for the day.

flashcards.front: Agent vs. principal vs. riskless principal
flashcards.back: Agent: matches, charges commission. Principal: trades from inventory, earns markup. Riskless principal: buys only after the customer's order, markup measured off contemporaneous cost.

quiz.stem: Regular-way settlement of a corporate stock transaction occurs:
options: On the same business day as the trade
Two business days after the trade date
One business day after the trade date
Three business days after the trade date
quiz.explanation: Regular-way settlement has been T+1 (one business day after the trade) since May 28, 2024. T+2 is the pre-2024 value and a classic stale-material trap; same-day is cash settlement; T+3 is the Reg T payment date, not settlement.

quiz.stem: A customer enters an order to sell 100 XYZ at 40 STOP. After entry the tape shows: 40.25, 40.10, 40.00, 39.85, 39.95. At what price is the order executed?
quiz.explanation: The print at 40.00 is at the stop, so the order is elected and becomes a market order; it then executes at the NEXT print, 39.85. Choosing 40.00 confuses election with execution; 39.95 would be relevant only for a stop-limit at 39.90 or lower.

quiz.stem: At 1:15 pm ET the S&P 500 is down 7% from the previous close. Under the market-wide circuit-breaker rules:
options: Trading continues; a halt occurs only at a 13% decline
Trading halts for the remainder of the day
Trading in all equity markets halts for 15 minutes
Only the S&P 500 stocks are paused for 5 minutes
quiz.explanation: A Level 1 (−7%) or Level 2 (−13%) breach before 3:25 pm ET triggers a 15-minute market-wide halt. Closing for the day is the Level 3 (−20%) consequence; the 5-minute single-stock pause describes LULD, a different system.

quiz.stem: An officer of a public company buys 1,000 shares in January and sells them at a $4,000 profit in April of the same year. Under Section 16(b):
options: The trade is legal because the officer held the shares for several months
The issuer may recover the $4,000 profit, regardless of the officer's intent
The SEC will impose a treble-damage penalty of $12,000 for insider trading
No consequence follows unless the officer used material nonpublic information
quiz.explanation: The short-swing profit rule lets the issuer recover any profit from a purchase and sale within 6 months, with no need to prove intent or misuse of information. Treble damages and the MNPI requirement belong to insider-trading law, which is a separate matter from the no-fault 16(b) clawback.

quiz.stem: The inside market for an OTC equity is 30.00 - 30.20. A firm with no position receives a customer order to buy 300 shares, buys 300 from a market maker at 30.20, and immediately resells them to the customer at 30.50. Under Rule 2121, the markup is:
options: Approximately 0.99%
Approximately 1.64%
Approximately 1.67%
Not measured as a percentage, because the firm acted as principal
quiz.explanation: This is a riskless principal trade, so the markup is measured off the firm's contemporaneous cost of $30.20: (30.50 − 30.20) / 30.20 = 0.99%. Measuring against the bid (30.00) gives the 1.64% trap; the point is that the base is what the firm just paid, not the inside bid or old inventory.

quiz.stem: A customer has two open GTC orders in XYZ: buy 100 at a limit of 50.00 and sell 100 at a limit of 55.00. XYZ goes ex-dividend for a $0.125 cash dividend with no DNR instruction. On the ex-date the orders are adjusted to:
options: Buy limit reduced to 49.87; sell limit unchanged
Buy limit reduced to 49.88; sell limit unchanged
Both orders reduced by $0.125
Buy limit reduced to 49.875; sell limit reduced to 54.875
quiz.explanation: Only below-market (BLiSS) orders are reduced on the ex-date; the buy limit is below the market and the sell limit above it, so only the buy limit changes. 50.00 − 0.125 = 49.875, rounded DOWN to the next valid tick = 49.87. Rounding up (49.88) or adjusting the above-market sell limit are the traps.

quiz.stem: A FINRA member internalizes a customer trade in an NYSE-listed stock away from the exchange. Within what time must it report the trade to a Trade Reporting Facility (TRF)?
options: Within 15 minutes
Within 10 seconds
By 8:00 pm the same day
By the next business day
quiz.explanation: Off-exchange trades in listed (NMS) stocks are reported to a TRF within 10 seconds of execution. The 15-minute answer is the TRACE/RTRS standard for bonds, and the next-business-day answer describes CAT order-event reporting — different facilities with different clocks.

quiz.stem: Which order qualifier requires immediate execution in whole or in part, with any unfilled portion canceled?
options: Fill-or-kill (FOK)
Immediate-or-cancel (IOC)
All-or-none (AON)
Good-till-canceled (GTC)
quiz.explanation: IOC allows partial fills and cancels the remainder immediately. FOK demands the ENTIRE order at once or nothing (no partials); AON demands the entire order but may wait; GTC concerns duration, not immediacy.
